title: Practical Exercises
summary: Four preparation exercises for the CCAR-F exam, solved the way a senior solutions architect would: step by step, with complete code and explicit justification for every design decision.

exercises.title: Multi-tool agent with escalation logic
exercises.objective: Design an agentic loop with MCP tool integration, structured error handling, and a deterministic control point that diverts sensitive operations to a human escalation flow.

subsections.title: Objective summary

blocks.content: This exercise practices five competencies that the certification evaluates together, not separately: (1) writing MCP tool descriptions that disambiguate similar cases, (2) understanding how the Agent SDK internally handles the `tool_use` → `tool_result` loop governed by `stop_reason`, (3) structuring tool errors with MCP's `isError` flag and an actionable category so the model can reason about them instead of just failing, (4) using a native Agent SDK hook — not a hand-rolled interceptor function — to insert a **deterministic** business rule that doesn't depend on the model deciding to follow it via prompt, and (5) verifying the final result through the `ResultMessage` the session exposes. The use case is a support agent with the ability to issue refunds, where a refund above a threshold must escalate to a human without exception.

subsections.title: Step 1 — Real MCP tools with createSdkMcpServer

blocks.content: The official scenario talks about "custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools," not native Messages API tools — the distinction matters because MCP defines its own error pattern (`isError`, see Step 3) and a qualified naming convention (`mcp__<server>__<tool>`). The Agent SDK offers `createSdkMcpServer` + `tool()` to declare an **in-process** MCP server: it runs inside the same application, without spinning up a separate subprocess, but the model sees it exactly as it would see any other MCP server. The same four familiar tools — `check_order_status`, `process_refund`, `issue_partial_credit`, `escalate_to_human` — with the same explicit disambiguation between the two that 'return money to the customer'.

blocks.label: mcp/support-server.ts

blocks.title: Why this disambiguation and not another
blocks.content: The general principle: **the tool description is the only channel through which the model understands when to use it** — there's no intent validation before selection. When two tools share a domain (both 'return money to the customer'), each description has to explicitly declare the negative boundary ('do NOT use for...') and not just the positive one. A selection error between `process_refund` and `issue_partial_credit` isn't a code bug, it's a specification bug: the fix lives in the tool's text, not in the system prompt.

subsections.title: Step 2 — How stop_reason governs the loop, inside and outside the SDK

blocks.content: The underlying principle is the same whether you use the raw Messages API or the Agent SDK: `stop_reason` is the only source of truth about whether to keep executing tools or present the final response — the end of the task is never inferred from text heuristics ("if the response mentions 'done'..."). With `tool_use` the requested tools get executed and reinjected as `tool_result`; with `end_turn` the final response is returned. A manual loop against the Messages API exposes `stop_reason` on every intermediate response — that's how you'd implement it from scratch. The Agent SDK runs exactly that same mechanism internally within `query()`, but **doesn't expose `stop_reason` on every turn**: it only appears in the final `SDKResultMessage`, when `message.type === "result"`.

blocks.label: The mechanism underneath (illustrative, you don't write this)
agent/run.ts — consuming query() from the caller's side

blocks.title: Why the distinction matters even though the mechanism is the same
blocks.content: The exam evaluates the `stop_reason` concept (Domain 1, Task 1.1) independently of which layer exposes it — a candidate has to recognize the signal in the raw Messages API **and** know that the Agent SDK abstracts it into an `SDKResultMessage` instead of removing it. Confusing 'the SDK handles the loop for me' with 'I don't need to understand stop_reason' is the most common comprehension error here: the cutoff mechanism is still the same, only the point where it's observed changes.

subsections.title: Step 3 — MCP's isError + the four error categories, not three

blocks.content: MCP already defines the low-level mechanism: a failing tool returns `isError: true` instead of throwing a raw exception, and the error content goes in the same `content` array as a successful result (see `check_order_status` in Step 1, which already uses this pattern). But `isError: true` alone doesn't tell the model **what to do** — a timeout, invalid input, a business policy violation, and a denied permission are completely different failures that demand completely different responses. On top of `isError`, the response needs one of four possible categories — `transient` / `validation` / `business` / `permission` — not three: `business` and `permission` aren't the same thing, and confusing them is the most common categorization error in this kind of design.

rows: transient
Timeout connecting to the payment gateway
Yes
Retry automatically, with backoff if there are several attempts
validation
`order_id` with invalid format
No (without fixing the input)
Fix the parameter and retry with the valid value
business
Refund above $500 — violates the approval policy, not an access permission
No
Escalate with `escalate_to_human`, never retry `process_refund` for that order
permission
Integration token without scope to write to the payment gateway
No
Don't retry — it's a credentials problem, not a customer request problem

blocks.label: agent/errors.ts

blocks.title: Why 'business' and 'permission' aren't interchangeable
blocks.content: A refund exceeding the approval threshold isn't a **permission** problem — the integration has full permission to call `process_refund`, the call simply violates a **business rule** (a policy on how much can be approved without human review). A real `permission` error would be, for example, a credential without the scope needed to write to the payment gateway — that's genuinely missing technical authorization. Labeling the first case as `permission` instead of `business` isn't a cosmetic detail: it changes what solution the person reading the log looks for (do I review credentials or do I review the approval policy?).

subsections.title: Step 4 — Native Agent SDK PreToolUse hook, not a hand-rolled interceptor

blocks.content: The rule "refunds above $500 require human review" **can't live only in the system prompt**: a prompt is a probabilistic instruction the model may not follow under conversational pressure (jailbreak, ambiguity, or plain sampling variability). The Agent SDK exposes this control point as a first-class hook — `PreToolUse` — that runs before the tool executes and can deny the call by returning `permissionDecision: "deny"` along with a reason the model reads. There's no need to write your own interception layer: the mechanism is already part of the SDK.

blocks.label: agent/hooks.ts

blocks.content: The hook is registered on `options.hooks.PreToolUse` with a `matcher` that limits it to the tool's qualified name (`mcp__support__process_refund` — see Step 1 on why MCP tools are exposed with that prefix), as set up in Step 2 inside `runSupportAgent`.

blocks.title: Why an SDK hook and not your own interceptor function
blocks.content: Writing a function that wraps the tool's execution achieves the same functional result, but it's not what the certification evaluates: Task Statement 1.5 explicitly asks to **apply Agent SDK hooks** for this pattern — `PreToolUse` to block before execution, `PostToolUse` to transform a result after the tool ran. Using the native mechanism also gives you something a custom function doesn't give for free: the hook applies uniformly to every point in the system that invokes that tool, without depending on every call site remembering to wrap the call.

subsections.title: Step 5 — Testing with multi-problem requests, verified via ResultMessage

blocks.content: The test case that validates the whole design together: a message that packs two requests of different nature into a single sentence. The agent must decompose it, resolve each part with the correct tool, and synthesize a single response — without mixing the results or resolving only the first half of the request. Verification no longer inspects `stop_reason` turn by turn (the SDK doesn't expose it there, see Step 2) — it's done against the final `SDKResultMessage` and the intermediate `assistant`/`user` messages `query()` itself emits.

blocks.label: agent/run.test.ts

blocks.title: Why this specific test case
blocks.content: A single problem per message doesn't exercise the agent's decomposition ability or the interaction between the loop and the hook under parallel calls. Combining a case that passes the business rule with one that triggers it in the same turn verifies three things at once: that the agent correctly parallelizes the two `process_refund` calls, that the `PreToolUse` hook blocks only the one that should be blocked without affecting the other, and that the final synthesis reports both results distinctly instead of collapsing them into a single generic conclusion.

subsections.title: Common mistakes and antipatterns to avoid

items.title: Reimplementing with a custom interceptor instead of an SDK hook
items.body: Wrapping the tool's execution with a custom function achieves the same functional result, but it's not what Task Statement 1.5 evaluates — the `PreToolUse` hook is the first-class mechanism for this, and using it gives consistency across every point in the system that invokes the tool.

items.title: Validating the business rule against the model's input
items.body: If the hook reads the amount from `tool_input.amount` instead of looking it up in the database, an adversarial prompt can make the model declare a false amount and evade the threshold. The rule should always be validated against a source of truth the model doesn't control.

items.title: Confusing 'permission' with 'business'
items.body: A refund exceeding the approval threshold is a business policy error, not a technical permission error — the integration does have permission to call the tool. Collapsing both categories into one hides whether the problem is credentials or policy.

items.title: Native Messages API tools disguised as 'MCP tools'
items.body: The official scenario explicitly calls for MCP tools. Declaring them as `Anthropic.Tool[]` without an MCP server in between loses the `isError` pattern and the qualified naming convention (`mcp__server__tool`) the exam expects you to recognize.

items.title: Assuming stop_reason disappears when using the Agent SDK
items.body: The SDK is still governed by `stop_reason` internally — it just exposes it in the final `SDKResultMessage` (`message.type === 'result'`), not on every intermediate turn like the raw Messages API.

items.title: Tool descriptions that only say what they do, not when not to use them
items.body: With overlapping-domain tools (two ways to 'return money'), omitting the explicit negative boundary ('do NOT use for...') is the most common cause of incorrect tool selection in production.

exercises.title: Configuring Claude Code for a team workflow
exercises.objective: Practice configuring CLAUDE.md hierarchies, path-specific rules, isolated skills with context: fork, project- and user-level MCP server integration, and when plan mode adds real value.

subsections.title: Objective summary

blocks.content: This exercise practices configuring Claude Code as a team tool, not for individual use: instructions applied consistently to everyone (CLAUDE.md), instructions that only activate when relevant to avoid noise (`rules/` with glob), an isolated and reusable unit of work (skill with `context: fork`), the coexistence of shared and personal configuration in MCP, and the criterion for deciding when plan mode adds real value instead of friction.

subsections.title: Step 1 — Project CLAUDE.md with universal standards

blocks.content: The CLAUDE.md at the root of the repo is the only instruction loaded in **every** Claude Code session on that project, no matter which file is being touched — that's why it should only contain what genuinely applies always: build/test commands, non-negotiable code conventions, and the team's testing policy. Area-specific detail (e.g. conventions only for `src/api/`) doesn't go here — it goes in `rules/` (Step 2), because always loading it would be noise for the 90% of sessions that don't touch that area.

blocks.label: CLAUDE.md
blocks.content:
# CLAUDE.md

This file guides Claude Code in this repository. It applies to **every**
session, no matter which part of the code is being edited.

## Commands

```bash
npm run dev       # Development server
npm test          # Full test suite (Vitest)
npm run lint      # ESLint + Prettier check
npm run build     # Production build — must pass without warnings
```

## Code conventions (apply to the whole repo)

- Strict TypeScript (`strict: true`) — don't use `any` without a comment
  justifying why it can't be typed.
- React functional components with hooks, not classes.
- kebab-case file names; PascalCase component names.
- No commit may drop test coverage below 80%.

## Testing (non-negotiable)

- Every business logic change requires a test covering it in the same
  commit — not in a later one.
- Run `npm test` before proposing any PR. If it fails, fix the root
  cause, never skip the test with `.skip`.

## Area-specific conventions

See `.claude/rules/` — loaded automatically only when editing files that
match their pattern, to avoid bloating the context of sessions that don't
need them.

blocks.title: Why here and not in rules/
blocks.content: General principle: **the cost of an instruction in CLAUDE.md is that it's paid in every session, whether it touches it or not**. What's genuinely universal (how to run the tests, the typing standard) justifies that fixed cost. Everything else is a candidate to move to a mechanism that loads conditionally — which is exactly what `rules/` solves.

subsections.title: Step 2 — Path-scoped rules in .claude/rules/

blocks.content: Each file in `.claude/rules/` declares in its YAML frontmatter the file glob patterns it applies to (`paths`). Claude Code loads that rule into the session only when the file being edited matches one of those patterns — that way API conventions don't pollute the context of a session that's only touching tests, and vice versa.

blocks.label: .claude/rules/api-conventions.md
blocks.content:
---
description: Endpoint design and error handling conventions in the API layer
paths:
  - "src/api/**/*"
---

# API Conventions

- Every new endpoint must validate the body with the corresponding Zod
  schema before touching the database.
- Domain errors are thrown as subclasses of `ApiError`, never as a
  generic `throw new Error(string)` — the error middleware relies on the
  type to map the correct HTTP status code.
- No handler should perform more than one N+1 query; use the DataLoaders
  already defined in `src/api/loaders/`.

blocks.label: .claude/rules/testing-conventions.md
blocks.content:
---
description: Structure and naming conventions for test files
paths:
  - "**/*.test.*"
  - "**/*.spec.*"
---

# Testing Conventions

- One `describe` per function/component under test, never a file with
  multiple unrelated top-level `describe` blocks.
- Name each `it` as a behavior statement ("returns null when the input
  is empty"), not "test 1", "test 2".
- Mock only the system's external boundaries (network, filesystem,
  clock) — never mock internal modules of the repo itself.

To verify the scoping works: asking Claude Code to edit a file in `src/api/orders.ts`, the `api-conventions.md` rule should show up reflected in its reasoning (it mentions DataLoaders, ApiError); asking it to edit `src/utils/format.ts` with no tests involved, that same rule shouldn't influence the response.

blocks.title: Why glob-scoping instead of everything in CLAUDE.md
blocks.content: The principle is the same as RAG applied to instructions: **loading only the context relevant to the current task reduces noise and improves precision**, instead of forcing the model to mentally filter out irrelevant instructions on every turn. Additionally, at the team level, splitting by path lets the owner of each area (API, testing, infra) maintain their own rule without having to coordinate edits on a single monolithic CLAUDE.md.

subsections.title: Step 3 — Project skill with context: fork and allowed-tools

blocks.content: A project-scoped skill lives at `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` and is invoked explicitly (`/skill-name`). `context: fork` makes the skill run in an isolated sub-conversation — it doesn't inherit or pollute the main conversation's history — and `allowed-tools` restricts what it can do, applying the principle of least privilege to a repeatable, well-defined task, like generating a changelog.

blocks.label: .claude/skills/changelog/SKILL.md
blocks.content:
---
name: changelog
description: Generates a CHANGELOG.md entry from the commits since the last tag
context: fork
allowed-tools: ["Bash(git log:*)", "Bash(git tag:*)", "Read", "Edit(CHANGELOG.md)"]
argument-hint: "[version]"
---

Generate a new entry in CHANGELOG.md for version `$1` (or the next semver
version if not specified), based on `git log` from the last tag to HEAD.

1. Run `git tag --sort=-creatordate | head -1` to find the last tag.
2. Run `git log <last-tag>..HEAD --oneline` to list the commits.
3. Group the commits into Added / Fixed / Changed based on their
   conventional prefix (feat/fix/refactor).
4. Insert the new entry at the top of CHANGELOG.md, respecting the
   Keep a Changelog format already used in the file.

Don't touch any file outside CHANGELOG.md.

To verify the isolation: running `/changelog` in the middle of a long debugging session shouldn't make the main session's summary mention anything about the internal changelog-generation process — the skill runs, produces its result, and the main thread continues as if it only received the final output.

blocks.title: Why context: fork and scoped allowed-tools
blocks.content: General principle: a task that **doesn't need** the conversation's full history (generating a changelog from git log) also shouldn't be able to affect it — `context: fork` is context isolation, not just organization. `allowed-tools` applies that same principle to capabilities: a changelog skill has no reason to have `Bash(rm:*)` or `Edit` over arbitrary files, so that surface isn't even offered to it.

subsections.title: Step 4 — Project-level and user-level MCP, simultaneously

blocks.content: `.mcp.json` at the repo root is team configuration: it's version-controlled, and credentials are referenced via environment variable expansion instead of being hardcoded in the file. `~/.claude.json` is the developer's personal configuration — for example, an experimental MCP server that isn't ready to be imposed on the rest of the team yet. Both scopes load at once: it's not 'one or the other'.

blocks.label: .mcp.json (repo root, version-controlled)
~/.claude.json (developer's personal config, not version-controlled)

blocks.content: To verify they coexist: opening Claude Code in the repo with both files present, `/mcp` should list three available servers — `postgres` and `github` (from the team's `.mcp.json`) alongside `my-experimental-linter` (personal) — with neither overriding the other.

blocks.title: Why separate scopes instead of a single file
blocks.content: The principle is to separate **configuration that defines the team's contract** (which servers the project needs to function, with credentials injected via environment so they aren't leaked into the repo) from **individual exploration configuration** (a server a developer is trying out that shouldn't appear for everyone else). Mixing them into a single version-controlled file would force a choice between exposing personal experiments to the whole team or being unable to experiment without touching shared configuration.

subsections.title: Step 5 — Plan mode vs. direct execution based on complexity

blocks.content: Plan mode has a cost (an extra round of alignment before touching code) and a benefit (avoids executing the wrong approach on a problem where more than one valid approach exists). The criterion isn't 'always use it' or 'never' but evaluating, for each task, whether that cost pays for itself.

rows: Renaming an internal function in a single file
No — direct execution
A single correct implementation path; no ambiguity to align on. Plan mode here only adds a round of friction without reducing risk.
Migrating a library used across 40 files (e.g. moment → date-fns)
Yes

There are multiple valid sequencing strategies (all at once vs. by module, with or without a temporary compatibility layer) and the blast radius is large — aligning the plan before touching 40 files avoids redoing work.
New feature with more than one reasonable implementation approach (e.g. in-memory cache vs. Redis)
Yes
The problem isn't 'how to write the code' but 'which architecture to choose' — exactly the kind of decision that benefits from being discussed explicitly before committing to code.

blocks.title: Why this criterion and not a fixed rule
blocks.content: The general principle: plan mode adds value when there's **genuine ambiguity of approach**, not simply when there's 'work to do'. A large task with a single obvious path (e.g. applying the same mechanical rename across 40 files) doesn't need plan mode as much as its size might suggest — what triggers the value of planning isn't the volume of change, it's the number of open design decisions.

subsections.title: Common mistakes and antipatterns to avoid

items.title: Putting area-specific conventions in the root CLAUDE.md
items.body: Bloats every session's context with rules irrelevant to most tasks. If a convention only applies to a folder or file type, it belongs in `.claude/rules/` with its corresponding `paths`.

items.title: Hardcoding credentials in a version-controlled .mcp.json
items.body: The file gets committed to the repo — any literal secret there is exposed in git history. Always use environment variable expansion (`${VAR}`) and keep the real value out of version control.

items.title: Skills without scoped allowed-tools
items.body: A skill that inherits full access to every tool loses the isolation guarantee that `context: fork` only half-provides — the context is isolated, but the actions can still have a blast radius as wide as the main conversation's.

items.title: Using plan mode reflexively for every 'big' task
items.body: A task's size isn't the right criterion; ambiguity of approach is. Forcing plan mode on a mechanical 40-file rename only adds friction without reducing any real risk.

items.title: A single giant CLAUDE.md instead of hierarchy + rules
items.body: As the team grows, a monolithic CLAUDE.md becomes hard to maintain without edit conflicts between owners of different areas — the hierarchy (project → path rules → skills) exists to distribute that ownership.

exercises.title: Structured data extraction pipeline
exercises.objective: Practice designing JSON schemas with nullable fields, validation-retry loops, few-shot prompting, batch processing with the Message Batches API, and routing to human review based on confidence.

subsections.title: Objective summary

blocks.content: This exercise practices the full cycle of a production extraction pipeline: a schema that explicitly distinguishes 'this isn't in the document' from 'I couldn't classify this', a retry loop that only retries what a retry can actually fix, few-shot to cover real structural variety, batch processing with individual failure handling, and a confidence mechanism that decides which extractions need a human before being trusted.

subsections.title: Step 1 — Schema with required, optional, enum+other, and nullable

blocks.content: The use case: extracting contract clauses. Three schema decisions separate a reliable pipeline from one that hallucinates: (1) fields that can legitimately be absent from the document are declared `nullable`, never simply `optional` — an optional field invites the model to omit it under uncertainty, a nullable one forces it to explicitly declare 'it's not there'; (2) closed categories use `enum` with an `other` option + a free-text detail field, so as not to force a false classification when no known category applies; (3) required fields are only the ones the document ALWAYS has by definition of the document type (e.g. the contract's parties), not the ones that are usually present.

blocks.label: schema.py

blocks.content: Running the pipeline against a batch of contracts where ~15% don't specify `termination_date` (indefinite contracts), the expected result is that those records return an explicit `termination_date: null` — not an invented date, nor the field absent from the JSON.

blocks.title: Why explicit-nullable and not absent-optional
blocks.content: When a field is simply optional in the schema, omitting it is a low-risk exit for the model under uncertainty — the result is indistinguishable from 'I didn't look for it' or 'I didn't understand it'. Forcing the field to always be present but nullable turns the uncertainty into an explicit, auditable signal: `null` means 'I looked and it's not there', not 'I didn't bother looking'. The same principle applies to the enum+other pattern: it forces the model to declare when the closed taxonomy isn't enough, instead of forcing an incorrect classification into the closest category.

subsections.title: Step 2 — Validation-retry loop that distinguishes error types

blocks.content: Not every validation failure deserves the same treatment. A format mismatch (a date as "March 2024" instead of ISO 8601) is fixable with a retry that shows the specific error. Missing information in the source (the model can't fill in `parties` because the document is cut off) doesn't get fixed by retrying with the same text — insisting would just generate pressure to invent a value.

blocks.label: extract.py
blocks.content:
from pydantic import ValidationError
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
MAX_RETRIES = 2

UNRECOVERABLE_HINTS = ("incomplete document", "not legible", "missing page")

def extract_with_retry(document_text: str) -> ContractExtraction | None:
    messages = [{
        "role": "user",
        "content": f"Extract the fields from the following contract:\n\n{document_text}",
    }]

    for attempt in range(MAX_RETRIES + 1):
        response = client.messages.create(
            model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
            max_tokens=2048,
            tools=[tool_schema],
            tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "extract_contract"},
            messages=messages,
        )
        tool_use = next(b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use")

        try:
            return ContractExtraction.model_validate(tool_use.input)
        except ValidationError as e:
            if attempt == MAX_RETRIES:
                log_unrecoverable(document_text, e)
                return None

            # Is the error about format (fixable) or does it indicate
            # genuinely missing information in the source (not fixable
            # with a retry)?
            error_text = str(e)
            if any(h in document_text.lower() for h in UNRECOVERABLE_HINTS):
                log_unrecoverable(document_text, e)
                return None

            # Targeted retry: the model is shown its own failed extraction
            # and the specific error, not just "try again".
            messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
            messages.append({
                "role": "user",
                "content": (
                    f"The previous extraction didn't pass schema validation:\n"
                    f"{error_text}\n\n"
                    f"Fix only the flagged field(s), keeping the rest of the "
                    f"extraction unchanged."
                ),
            })

    return None

blocks.title: Why differentiate before retrying
blocks.content: Blindly retrying on any validation failure wastes tokens and, worse, increases the chance the model 'solves' a case with no real information by inventing a plausible value just to pass validation on the next attempt. The principle: **retrying is only the right tool when the error is about form, not substance** — a format mismatch is about form (the data is there, expressed wrong); an incomplete source is about substance (the data simply isn't there).

subsections.title: Step 3 — Few-shot for real structural variety

blocks.content: A single few-shot example style (e.g. always bibliography-format citations) leaves the model without a reference when the real document uses inline citations or mixes narrative text with tables. The examples must cover the format variety that actually exists in the real document set, not just the most common case.

blocks.label: few_shot_examples.py
blocks.content:
FEW_SHOT_EXAMPLES = [
    {
        # Case 1: inline citations within narrative text.
        "document": (
            "The tenant (Juan Pérez) agrees to pay $1,200 monthly as "
            "established in clause 4.2 of this contract, effective from "
            "January 1, 2024 with no defined termination date."
        ),
        "extraction": {
            "parties": [{"name": "Juan Pérez", "role": "tenant", "role_detail": None}],
            "contract_type": "lease",
            "contract_type_detail": None,
            "termination_date": None,  # 'no termination date' -> explicit null
            "penalty_clause_amount_usd": None,
            "governing_law": None,
        },
    },
    {
        # Case 2: information in a structured table, not prose.
        "document": (
            "TERMS TABLE\n"
            "| Field              | Value               |\n"
            "| Buyer              | Acme Corp           |\n"
            "| Seller             | Beta Ltd            |\n"
            "| Type               | Asset purchase      |\n"
            "| Governing law      | Delaware, USA       |"
        ),
        "extraction": {
            "parties": [
                {"name": "Acme Corp", "role": "buyer", "role_detail": None},
                {"name": "Beta Ltd", "role": "seller", "role_detail": None},
            ],
            "contract_type": "purchase",
            "contract_type_detail": None,
            "termination_date": None,
            "penalty_clause_amount_usd": None,
            "governing_law": "Delaware, USA",
        },
    },
]

# These are injected as real user/assistant turns before the document to
# extract, not as descriptive text within the system prompt — the model
# generalizes better from format examples than from a description of
# formatting rules.

blocks.title: Why two different formats and not two examples of the same type
blocks.content: The value of few-shot isn't 'showing examples', it's **narrowing the variation the model has to generalize on its own**. Two narrative-prose examples teach extraction from narrative prose, but give no signal about how to read a table — the model would have to generalize that jump unsupported. Covering the formats that genuinely appear in the corpus (narrative, table, numbered clauses) is what reduces errors in production, not the total number of examples.

subsections.title: Step 4 — Batch processing with the Message Batches API

blocks.content: For 100 documents, the Message Batches API lets you send all requests as a single asynchronous job, with up to 50% discount over standard pricing and without consuming the synchronous rate limit. Each request carries its own `custom_id` so each result (or failure) can be mapped back to its source document.

blocks.label: batch_pipeline.py

blocks.title: Why batch and not 100 synchronous calls
blocks.content: The principle: when the task **doesn't require a real-time response** (an extraction pipeline running against a nightly batch, not an interactive chat), the synchronous API is the wrong tool — it pays synchronous rate limits and the full price for latency nobody's waiting on. Handling by `custom_id` is what makes it safe to retry only what failed: resending the entire batch for 3 failures out of 100 would waste 97% of the cost and time already invested.

subsections.title: Step 5 — Per-field confidence and routing to human review

blocks.content: Asking the model for a confidence score per field (not a single global one) allows routing exactly the portion of the extraction that needs it to human review, instead of the whole document. Analyzing resulting accuracy by document type and by field (not just an aggregate accuracy) is what reveals whether the pipeline systematically fails on a subset — for example, scanned contracts with poor OCR quality.

blocks.label: confidence_routing.py

blocks.title: Why segment instead of trusting a global accuracy
blocks.content: An aggregate accuracy of 88% can perfectly well hide a segment at 60% offset by another at 98% — the global figure doesn't say where to intervene. Routing by field confidence, instead of by whole document, applies the same principle at the operational decision level: sending only `termination_date` of a document to human review when the rest of the fields had high confidence is cheaper and more precise than routing the entire document over a single doubtful field.

subsections.title: Common mistakes and antipatterns to avoid

items.title: Optional fields instead of required-nullable
items.body: A field the model can simply omit under uncertainty is indistinguishable from a field that wasn't looked for. Forcing presence + explicit null turns uncertainty into an auditable signal.

items.title: Retrying without differentiating the failure type
items.body: Retrying the same way on a format error and on genuinely missing source information pressures the model to invent a value just to pass validation on the second attempt.

items.title: Few-shot with a single document style
items.body: Examples that cover only the most common format give the model no signal on how to generalize to tables, inline citations, or numbered clauses if those formats also appear in the real corpus.

items.title: Resubmitting an entire batch for partial failures
items.body: Without handling by `custom_id`, a 3% failure rate forces reprocessing 100% of the batch, wasting the cost and time already invested in the 97% that succeeded.

items.title: Global confidence instead of per-field, and aggregate accuracy instead of per-segment
items.body: Both hide where the real problem is: a global confidence score routes entire documents when only one field is doubtful, and an aggregate accuracy hides that the pipeline systematically fails on a specific subset (e.g. scanned documents).

exercises.title: Designing and debugging a multi-agent research pipeline
exercises.objective: Practice coordinator-subagent orchestration, parallel execution via Task, structured output with provenance tracing, error propagation, and synthesis of conflicting sources.

subsections.title: Objective summary

blocks.content: This exercise practices the coordinator-subagent (hub-and-spoke) pattern for research: a coordinator that delegates in parallel to specialized subagents, a finding format that separates content from provenance so attribution isn't lost during synthesis, structured error propagation when a subagent partially fails, and an explicit policy for how to handle sources that contradict each other.

subsections.title: Step 1 — Coordinator with Task in allowedTools and explicit per-subagent context

blocks.content: The coordinator needs `Task` enabled in its `allowedTools` to be able to invoke subagents. The key design decision: each subagent receives its instructions and the context it needs **directly in the invocation prompt**, not through automatic inheritance of the coordinator's history — subagents in this pattern don't see the full conversation, only what's explicitly passed to them.

blocks.label: coordinator/agents.ts

blocks.title: Why explicit context and not automatic inheritance
blocks.content: General principle: automatic context inheritance couples the subagent to the coordinator's full history, including noise irrelevant to its sub-task — and makes the subagent's behavior depend on the point in the conversation where it was invoked, which is hard to test and reproduce. Passing context explicitly in the `Task` prompt makes every invocation self-contained: you can test the subagent with that same prompt in isolation, and the coordinator controls exactly what information crosses the boundary into each subagent.

subsections.title: Step 2 — Parallel execution via multiple Task calls in one response

blocks.content: When sub-questions are independent of each other (none depends on another's result), the coordinator should emit all `Task` calls in the same turn so they run in parallel, instead of waiting for one's result before launching the next.

blocks.label: coordinator/parallel-vs-sequential.ts

blocks.title: Why parallelize only when there's real independence
blocks.content: The principle isn't 'parallelize whenever technically possible', but to parallelize when the sub-tasks are **causally independent**. Forcing parallelism between a sub-question that depends on another's result would break the research (the second subagent would start without the information it needs). The coordinator's prompt has to encode that dependency criterion, not just the generic instruction to 'be fast'.

subsections.title: Step 3 — Structured output that separates content from provenance

blocks.content: Every finding from a subagent must carry its claim, the textual evidence excerpt that supports it, the exact source (URL or document name), and the publication date — as separate fields, not mixed into a narrative paragraph. That's what lets the synthesis subagent preserve attribution when combining findings from multiple sources.

blocks.label: agents/finding-schema.ts

blocks.title: Why separate fields and not a narrative summary per finding
blocks.content: If the research subagent returns a narrative paragraph directly ("according to Gartner, adoption grew..."), the synthesis subagent has to re-parse that prose to recover the source before it can cite it correctly when combining multiple findings — and it's easy to lose or mix up attributions during that re-parsing. Keeping `claim`, `evidence_excerpt`, `source`, and `published_date` as separate fields from the start eliminates that re-extraction step and the loss of provenance it involves.

subsections.title: Step 4 — Structured subagent error propagation

blocks.content: When a subagent fails (timeout, tool error, or empty result), the coordinator needs to receive a structured error object — not a generic string — to be able to decide with judgment whether to continue with the partial results it does have, and to be able to annotate the final report with the real coverage gaps instead of presenting it as if it were complete.

blocks.label: coordinator/error-handling.ts

blocks.title: Why continue with partials instead of failing the whole pipeline
blocks.content: If a single subagent's timeout (out of, say, four) brought down the whole pipeline, one isolated failure would cost 100% of the work the others already completed. The principle is to **degrade gracefully and be honest about the degradation**: synthesize with what's available, but the final report explicitly states what couldn't be covered — the alternative (presenting a partial report as if it were complete) is worse than failing visibly, because it induces a false sense of full coverage in whoever reads it.

subsections.title: Step 5 — Synthesis with conflicting sources

blocks.content: When two credible sources report different statistics for the same fact, correct synthesis preserves both values with their attribution, and structures the report distinguishing well-established findings (multiple sources agree) from disputed ones (sources disagree) — never arbitrarily choosing one of the two values as 'the correct one'.

blocks.label: agents/synthesis-conflict.ts

blocks.title: Why preserve the conflict instead of resolving it automatically
blocks.content: Arbitrarily picking a value (the first one received, the one from the source that 'sounds' bigger) hides real information from the user: that the fact is disputed. The general principle is that **synthesis shouldn't invent certainty where there is none** — presenting both values with their source and a note on the possible cause of the discrepancy gives the reader the complete information to decide which to weight more according to their own judgment, instead of inheriting an implicit, undeclared decision made by the pipeline.

subsections.title: Common mistakes and antipatterns to avoid

items.title: Relying on automatic context inheritance between coordinator and subagents
items.body: Couples the subagent's behavior to the coordinator's full conversation history, making it harder to test the subagent in isolation and reproducibly.

items.title: Launching Task sequentially when sub-questions are independent
items.body: Wastes latency — two 20s subagents running in series cost 40s when they could cost ~20s in parallel, with no correctness benefit in exchange.

items.title: Findings as narrative prose instead of structured fields
items.body: Forces the synthesis subagent to re-parse free text to recover each claim's source, with high risk of losing or mixing up attributions when combining findings.

items.title: Letting a subagent's failure bring down the whole pipeline
items.body: An isolated timeout shouldn't cost 100% of the work already completed by the other subagents — the correct response is to degrade with partial results and declare the gap, not fail everything.

items.title: Arbitrarily choosing between conflicting sources
items.body: Averaging, keeping the first value received, or 'picking the source that sounds more reliable' without declaring it hides from the user that the fact is disputed — synthesis should preserve the conflict explicitly, not resolve it silently.
